newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Go-Ahead sets sights on overseas deals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Go-Ahead sets sights on overseas deals.

text.p: British transporter Go-Ahead Group Plc has set its sights on expansion into rail and buses on the European continent in a bid to keep up with the sector's explosive growth which has trebled its shareprice within three years.

Overseas expansion is seen as a crucial next step for transport firms like Go-Ahead which have enjoyed a boom on the back of bus and rail deregulation and privatisation under the Conservative government. But with that process almost completed and the benefits largely reaped, analysts say the sector is now looking for internationally-driven growth.
Chris Moyes, Go-Ahead's commercial director, told Reuters in an interview that the group was already "prospecting" for a deal in Poland and other central European countries.

The British buses-to-rail combine, which was confirmed as winner of the lucrative London Thameslink rail franchise on Tuesday, failed in its bid for Swebus of Sweden which was eventually clinched by rival Stagecoach.
But Moyes told Reuters that overseas expansion remained a top priority and plenty of other opportunities remained.
"We have a presence in Poland and are exploring possible partnerships with others. It could be in buses or rail.
"The potential of Poland or central Europe is the first likely step overseas -- but it could take a long time to come to fruition," he said.
He sees moves by countries on the continent to cut budget deficits in a bid to enter the single currency as a factor that will accelerate transport industry deregulation.
But one analyst offered a cautionary note on the drive to clinch deals in Europe.
"Overseas firms see British companies coming laden with their fat pockets of cash and the prices have been marked up accordingly," said Inigo Edsberg, from Panmure Gordon.
The sector still remains the shareholders' darling. But Edsberg added that after a good run, the time was ripe for investors to cash in some of their spoils.
"In general, given the picture in the (British) bus industry and that the TOC (train operating companies or rail franchises) sale is almost over, now is the time to take profits," he said.
At present Go-Ahead has no operations outside Britain. After clinching the Thameslink deal, Moyes said the group was "finely balanced" between buses and rail.

Go-Ahead has roughly eight percent of the British bus market, including a 1,000 strong fleet in London. Buses account for around 190 million pounds ($310.4 million) of annual turnover, with the Thameslink and Thames rail deals providing an extra 200 million, said Moyes.
Go-Ahead won the Thameslink franchise with French partner VIA-GTI, owning 65 percent and 35 percent of the GOVIA bid, respectively.

The GOVIA team will receive a 2.5 million pound subsidy in year one of its franchise, paying a premium of 28.4 million pounds to the government by 2004. The line's passenger revenue in the year ended March 31 1996 was 76 million pounds.
Bus and rail privatisation have helped power Go-Ahead's shares from their 120 pence open after flotation in May 1994 to 508 pence on Tuesday -- a rise of around 323 percent.

Go-Ahead has also outperformed the transport sector by 350 percent from its flotation to the end of January 1997. Against the FTSE All Share index, it has outperformed by 300 percent, according to the Reuters 3000 database.
Its return on equity is the highest in the sector at 62.3 percent. ($1=.6120 Pound)
